title: {{NAME}} and the Hero Who Forgot How
moral: Sometimes the greatest act of courage is admitting you need someone, and letting them in.

pages.content:
Volt City was the kind of place where the extraordinary was simply Tuesday. Its skyline was a grammar of towers and power lines and launch pads, and at any given moment six or seven superheroes were streaking across the sky trailing their signatures: columns of lightning, rings of force, ribbons of light.

{{NAME}} arrived at the city's edge by train, stepping onto a platform where a sign read HERO DISTRICT, ALL VISITORS WELCOME. The district was a grid of workshops and launch bays and what appeared to be a very busy café.

But something was wrong with the sky.

Not the weather. The heroes. They were flying in circles. Overlapping, uncertain circles, like birds before a storm. And at the very top of the tallest tower, a figure sat alone on a ledge, enormous and motionless, made entirely of brushed steel and dark composite materials, with two bright eyes like twin blue headlamps.

Everyone in the plaza below was giving that tower a very wide berth. {{NAME}} walked toward it.

pages.content:
His name, {{NAME}} learned from a small child sitting on the plaza steps eating an apple, was Titan. And Titan had been the greatest superhero in Volt City for twenty-two years.

"He can't remember his power," the child said, as though this explained everything, because it did. "It happens sometimes. A hero takes too much damage in a big fight, and something gets disconnected. He just sits up there."

{{NAME}} looked up. Even from here, he could see the stillness of the figure on the ledge, and it wasn't the stillness of rest. It was the stillness of someone who had stopped trusting themselves.

He took the stairs, all forty-seven flights of them, which was a considerable commitment. He arrived breathing hard and sat down on the ledge beside Titan without preamble. The city spread below them like a circuit board that had learned to dream.

Titan's blue eyes turned toward him slowly. The robot's voice, when it came, was like the lowest key on a very old piano. "You are small," he said. "And uninvited."

"I know," said {{NAME}}, still catching his breath. "Forty-seven flights."

Titan regarded him for a long moment. Then: "Why?"

"Because you're up here," {{NAME}} said simply. "And everyone else isn't."

pages.content:
{{NAME}} didn't try to fix Titan. He understood, in a way he couldn't have explained, that trying to fix was the wrong approach entirely.

Instead he asked questions. The same kind of patient questions he asked his grandmother when she forgot where she had put things, gentle and specific. Not what did you lose, but tell me about the last time you had it.

"The last time you used your power," {{NAME}} said. "What were you thinking about?"

Titan was quiet for a long time. His chest made a sound like a subterranean generator. "I was thinking about the family in the building," he said finally. "The third floor. There was a child who reminded me of someone."

"Who?"

"Someone I once helped, years ago. A long time."

"And now?"

Another long pause. "I am afraid," Titan said, very quietly, "that the next time I am needed, I will not be enough."

Down in the city, the alarm began to sound. A bright, urgent pulsing that brought every hero in the sky to attention. A support structure on the northern bridge was failing. Fast.

Titan looked at the alarm. Then at {{NAME}}. And {{NAME}} saw the moment the robot made his choice.

pages.content:
Titan moved like a force of nature that had been holding its breath.

He launched from the ledge in a single motion and hit the sky with a sound like a thunderclap three seconds late. His headlamp eyes blazed. His power came back not all at once but in a rush, like memory returning the moment you stop straining for it.

{{NAME}} watched from the ledge, too high to do anything useful and completely unable to look away.

The northern bridge was swaying. Titan caught the failing beam with both arms and held. The bridge groaned. He held harder. Other heroes converged, adding their own strength to his, a dozen different powers working together while the city's engineers scrambled below.

Four minutes. Five. Six. Then the signal sounded: supports locked. Crisis contained.

Titan rose from the bridge slowly, and from forty-seven floors up, {{NAME}} could see his blue eyes from across the city, bright and steady. He raised one enormous hand.

It was, {{NAME}} thought, the clearest thing he had ever seen.

pages.content:
Titan came back to the ledge. He sat down beside {{NAME}} again, which, given the circumstances, felt like the right place to be.

His chest made a new sound. Not the subterranean generator sound. Something lighter, more like a hum that had stopped apologising for itself.

"The question you asked," Titan said. "About the last time I used my power. I had been asked it by a thousand technicians and diagnosticians." He paused. "None of them waited for the answer."

{{NAME}} didn't say anything. He leaned back and looked at the sky, which was clear and full of lights and entirely, completely itself.

The train home ran through the golden evening, and {{NAME}} sat by the window and watched Volt City recede, still flickering with life. He was home before dark, warm in his bed, the city's distant hum replaced by the quieter hum of his own neighbourhood.

His eyes were heavy and pleasant. He was nearly asleep when he thought of something. Titan had said, as {{NAME}} left: "Come back. I know something about this city that nobody has asked about yet."

There was always, {{NAME}} thought, more to find out.
